metadata.title: Premetric Structural Unification The Constraint-Governed Emergence of Geometry, Scalar Dynamics and Operational Relativity
metadata.description:
Premetric Structural Unification

The Constraint-Governed Emergence of Geometry, Scalar Dynamics, and Operational Relativity

An Integrated Cross-Corpus Lean Formalization

Overview

This paper presents an integrated formal account of how gravitational response, quantum evolution, inertial geometry, and operational relativity emerge from a common premetric constraint architecture.

The construction begins with the AASC Kernel of Admissibility And Standing Constraint. Its four roles - Admissibility, Standing, Reference, and Irreversibility - govern which descriptions remain answerable to an original occurrence and its warranted comparisons before metricity, duration, Hamiltonian evolution, or clock readings are selected.

Canonical L-metric licensing then determines which metric uses remain warranted through the declared continuations. Occupied physical preparations supply the inputs for three downstream derivations:

  • Einstein-form gravitational response;

  • free Schrödinger dynamics for an isolated scalar;

  • calibrated Lorentzian interval and operational clock geometry.

The result is a structural unification of three formalisms with a common premetric origin, while preserving the distinctions between their respective preparations, domains, calibrations, and uniqueness claims.

Central integrated result

The combined construction establishes that a common premetric constraint can support:

  • a canonically licensed metric description;

  • an Einstein-form first-response law;

  • a controlled nonflat Klein-Gordon evolution;

  • a stress tensor derived from the same scalar action;

  • a conditional sourced Einstein equation;

  • an isolated free quantum scalar evolution;

  • a maximal-domain generator for that evolution;

  • a calibrated Lorentzian interval;

  • native inertial geometry;

  • positive-rest clocks;

  • finite radar, ruler, and synchronization networks;

  • quantitative recovery estimates on their declared domains.

The three branches are not obtained by simply assuming the familiar formalisms. Each is derived from a different class of original observations and admissible preparations governed by the same premetric constraint discipline.

Premetric constraint and canonical metric licensing

The AASC Kernel begins with an identifiable occurrence and a use for which it can be held answerable.

Its four structural roles are:

  • Admissibility: what counts for the declared use;

  • Standing: whether the occurrence qualifies;

  • Reference: which occurrence is under discussion;

  • Irreversibility: what remains fixed when a completed use is taken up again.

At the AMetric boundary, a retained description must preserve the original distinctions required by the declared questions and continuations. Canonical L-metric licensing then determines the greatest safe region of metric uses that remains warranted under the original contract.

The paper distinguishes:

  • the Kernel from downstream physical realizations;

  • metric licensing from metric generation;

  • existence of a realization from uniqueness of a realization;

  • interface minimality from physical selection;

  • common governance from identification of separate branches.

The Kernel determines the structural requirements of determinate description, but does not by itself select the Einstein-Hilbert action, a particular scalar state, a numerical calibration, or a unique spacetime.

Einstein-form gravitational response

For gravity, the paper considers bounded metric operands and compact metric variations.

Agreement with the original readings on compact Lie variations forces a smooth natural local response to be divergence-free on every smooth metric. If a response has nonzero divergence at an occupied operand, a compactly supported Lie test witnesses the failure.

In four dimensions, the paper establishes that the least differential order of an active, closed, natural, metric-only symmetric response is two. Lovelock’s theorem then classifies every response attaining that minimum as an Einstein tensor term together with a constant metric term.

The Einstein-Hilbert action fixes the coefficients of these terms. The resulting response therefore has Einstein form within the declared comparison class and hypotheses.

The argument does not claim that AASC alone selects the Einstein-Hilbert action. Rather, once the admitted action and response class are supplied, the structural response tests force the Einstein-form normal form at the minimal active order.

Klein-Gordon evolution on a controlled nonflat metric

Holding the metric fixed in the same real scalar action yields the Klein-Gordon field equation at stationarity.

The paper constructs a controlled nonflat metric branch supporting real Klein-Gordon evolution for compact smooth central data. The analytic results include:

  • existence on a controlled interval;

  • uniqueness among arbitrary locally smooth competitors;

  • strong recovery on the protected causal domain;

  • quantitative field and metric estimates;

  • explicit domain restrictions;

  • continuity under the stated data topology.

The scalar construction is not merely a formal variation. The field, metric, source, domain, and causal support are tracked together under the declared premetric licensing conditions.

Same-action scalar stress and gravitational balance

The same scalar action is varied independently in two directions.

Holding the metric fixed gives the scalar field equation. Holding the field fixed gives the represented scalar stress.

Both variations act on the same perturbation of the same metric. When the total action is stationary under the complete class of metric variations, the scalar stress and Einstein-Hilbert response combine into the sourced Einstein equation.

This establishes a same-action gravitational balance for the constructed scalar field on the admitted geometry.

The argument preserves the distinction between:

  • the scalar field equation;

  • the metric response;

  • the represented stress;

  • Ward and exchange identities;

  • complete total metric stationarity;

  • the resulting sourced Einstein equation.

A jointly coupled Einstein-Klein-Gordon existence theorem beyond the stated construction remains outside the claim.

Free quantum scalar and Schrödinger dynamics

For the isolated complex scalar, mass-shell translations determine limiting complex packet amplitudes.

These amplitudes distinguish different separately continuous evolutions on the same carrier. Any evolution satisfying the declared continuity, translation, and packet-amplitude conditions must therefore coincide with the constructed free evolution.

The paper establishes:

  • the free evolution on the isolated scalar carrier;

  • the full generator;

  • its maximal domain;

  • phase-fixed transport;

  • uniqueness relative to the stated comparison class;

  • quantitative recovery from low-momentum data and controlled momentum tails.

The free Schrödinger law is thus obtained as the unique admissible first-response Hamiltonian form within the declared isolated scalar comparison class.

The result does not claim that the Kernel alone selects every quantum Hamiltonian or that all interacting quantum theories are thereby determined.

Emergence of inertial geometry and the Lorentz interval

For the inertial preparation, completed reach and rest comparisons transitive on the one-tick frontier determine a spatial quadratic form.

The original positive rest tick fixes the scale. Four travel-time readings per displacement pair then test the shape of the front independently of which individual operations the apparatus supplies.

The construction recovers:

  • a native inertial geometry;

  • a spatial quadratic form;

  • a calibrated Lorentz interval;

  • positive-rest clock behaviour;

  • coasting-clock comparisons;

  • synchronization procedures;

  • finite radar and ruler measurements.

The interval is recovered from the original operational comparisons rather than installed as a prior coordinate convention.

Quantitative recovery and operational apparatus

The paper includes explicit low-momentum and tail estimates for the quantum branch, together with local field and metric estimates for the classical branch.

The operational construction uses finite clock-and-ruler networks with:

  • positive-mass clocks;

  • recorded radar exchanges;

  • successful request domains;

  • waiting-time subtraction;

  • simultaneous endpoint selection;

  • ruler-length recovery;

  • synchronization procedures;

  • explicit first failures.

A failed operational request remains part of the declared use contract. A later successful request or repaired apparatus does not retroactively erase the original failure.

The measurement results are therefore tied to actual occupied preparations and declared apparatus domains rather than to an abstract coordinate system alone.

Joined structural realization

Theorem 10.1 traces the gravitational response, scalar evolution, quantum transport, inertial geometry, and clock measurements back to their licensed preparations.

The joined construction contains:

  • common premetric governance;

  • canonical L-metric licensing;

  • an admitted metric operand;

  • Einstein-form gravitational response;

  • controlled scalar evolution;

  • scalar stress from the same action;

  • free quantum evolution on an isolated branch;

  • calibrated inertial geometry;

  • operational clock and ruler readings;

  • quantitative recovery statements.

The result is a structural unification, not an identification of all branches as one physical object. The gravitational, classical scalar, quantum, and operational sectors retain their own comparison classes and hypotheses while sharing a common premetric source.

Formal verification and Lean record

The paper includes an integrated Lean formalization and a source-to-theorem map covering the principal structural, geometric, scalar, quantum, and operational declarations.

The formal record supports:

  • AASC Kernel and AMetric licensing interfaces;

  • metric-use and canonical-licensing constructions;

  • common-preparation maps;

  • Einstein-response classification;

  • scalar field and stress constructions;

  • free quantum-carrier and generator results;

  • inertial geometry and Lorentz comparison;

  • clock and finite-network operations;

  • quantitative recovery statements;

  • explicit scope and non-claim boundaries.

The paper distinguishes machine-checked formal declarations from analytic hypotheses, physical interpretation, and external mathematical inputs. Each application remains relative to its stated domains, calibration data, comparison class, and admissibility conditions.

Scope and realization boundary

The paper establishes:

  • a common premetric origin for three downstream formalisms;

  • canonical licensing of metric use;

  • Einstein-form minimal first-response classification;

  • controlled nonflat Klein-Gordon evolution;

  • same-action scalar stress and conditional gravitational balance;

  • isolated free Schrödinger dynamics;

  • generator and maximal-domain uniqueness;

  • calibrated Lorentz interval recovery;

  • native inertial geometry;

  • operational clock, radar, ruler, and synchronization constructions;

  • quantitative recovery on the stated domains;

  • an integrated cross-corpus Lean formalization.

It does not claim:

  • that AASC alone selects the Einstein-Hilbert action;

  • that AASC alone selects a particular scalar state or calibration;

  • a complete coupled Einstein-Klein-Gordon existence theorem;

  • a full quantum theory of gravity;

  • a full Standard Model or gauge-theoretic realization;

  • a unique physical projection among all faithful downstream realizations;

  • a unique spacetime;

  • a global interacting quantum-field limit;

  • universal physical validity beyond the declared comparison classes;

  • that the formalization eliminates the need for physical domain evidence.

The uniqueness results are always relative to the stated admissible class, original questions, comparison domain, calibration data, and continuity or regularity hypotheses.
